name: Apache Pig
summary: A step-by-step scripting language, Pig Latin, that compiles to MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs on Hadoop. Still released, but the project calls itself dormant.
intro: You write a Pig Latin script as a sequence of named steps: `LOAD` a file, `FILTER`, `GROUP`, `JOIN`, `FOREACH ... GENERATE`, then `STORE` the result. Pig runs on the client: it parses the script into a logical plan, optimizes it, and compiles it into a chain of MapReduce jobs (the default), a Tez DAG (`-x tez`) or Spark jobs (`-x spark`) that it submits to the cluster. Data stays in plain files in HDFS; load and store functions parse and write them, and no schema is required up front. Pig’s data model is nested (tuples, bags and maps), and user-defined functions in Java or Python plug into any step. The interactive Grunt shell and `-x local` mode run scripts on one machine for testing.

Pig is free under Apache 2.0 and is not retired, but it is barely moving. After 0.17.0 in June 2017 there was no release for eight years, until 0.18.0 in September 2025 added support for Hadoop 3, Tez 0.10, Spark 3, Hive 3, HBase 2 and Python 3. In its April 2026 board report the project described its status as “Dormant”, in maintenance mode with bug fixes and dependency updates, and no new committer since 2018. A 0.19.0 release was targeted for May 2026 but has not appeared. Amazon EMR still offers Pig, at version 0.17.0.
strengths: Readable dataflow scripts: each line is one transformation, which suits multi-step ETL better than one large SQL statement
Works on raw files with no schema or loading step, and handles nested data natively
UDFs in Java or Python plug into any step, and Pig can call Hive UDFs
Existing scripts can move from MapReduce to Tez or Spark by changing the `-x` flag
limits: Dormant: one release in eight years, no new committers since 2018, and maintenance limited to bug fixes and dependency updates
Docs lag the code: the 0.18.0 getting-started page still lists Hadoop 2.X and Java 1.7 as requirements
Tied to Hadoop: cluster modes need a Hadoop cluster and HDFS, and the local Tez and Spark modes are still marked experimental
Pig Latin is its own language, not SQL: analysts and BI tools can’t query data through Pig
Managed platforms lag too: Amazon EMR 7.14 ships Pig 0.17.0 from 2017

story: Internet companies such as Yahoo were analyzing terabytes of web crawls, search logs and click streams every day. Parallel databases such as Teradata could do it but were prohibitively expensive at web scale, and many of the people doing the analysis were procedural programmers who found SQL unnatural. Hadoop’s MapReduce was cheap and popular, but too low-level and rigid: a one-input, two-stage model that led to lots of custom code that was hard to maintain and reuse.

Christopher Olston, Benjamin Reed, Utkarsh Srivastava, Ravi Kumar and Andrew Tomkins at Yahoo Research designed Pig Latin to sit between the two: a sequence of high-level steps, each a single relational-style transformation, compiled into MapReduce jobs. The prototype won internal users, Yahoo built a production engineering team around it, and in September 2007 Pig entered the Apache Incubator. By June 2009 roughly 60% of Yahoo’s ad-hoc Hadoop jobs and 40% of its production Hadoop jobs were submitted through Pig.

Pig became a top-level Apache project in September 2010, at the same board meeting as Hive. It added Tez in 2014 and Spark in 2017 as faster engines, then went eight years without a release until 0.18.0 in 2025.

choices.choice: A dataflow of steps instead of one declarative query
choices.why: Yahoo’s programmers preferred writing step-by-step scripts. Using relational primitives such as FILTER and GROUP for each step still let the system reorder and optimize them.

choices.choice: Query raw files with no import step
choices.why: Ad-hoc analysis started from dumps of logs. Pig reads files in place through a user-supplied parsing function, so there is no loading phase, and other tools keep using the same files.
Programmers think in nested structures and much of the data on disk was already nested. Tuples, bags and maps avoided flattening everything into normalized tables.
Analysis at Yahoo needed custom logic such as spam detection or query expansion. Every Pig Latin operation can call user-defined functions, which use the same nested data model.
